title: Sasanian Mesopotamia
subtitle: 224–637 AD · The Heart of Ērānšahr — Ctesiphon the Imperial Capital, the Nahrawan and the Richest Land on Earth, the Church of the East and the Talmud, and the Arab Conquest

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Ardashir making the Sawad the empire's core, Shapur I and the captured Roman emperors, Shapur II's long war, the fifth-century disasters, Kavad and Mazdak, Khosrow I's great reforms, Khosrow II's last war, and the Arab conquest

entries.label: Ardashir I and the making of the Sawad
entries.hint: Ardashir destroyed the last Arsacid in 224, was crowned at Ctesiphon in 226, took Hatra around 240, and built a centralised empire — Ērānšahr, 'the domain of the Iranians' — where the Parthians had held a loose confederation. He kept the capital at Ctesiphon and made lowland Mesopotamia, the Sawad, the empire's directly-ruled core and its richest province. It stayed the heart of the state for four hundred years.
entries.note: al-Tabari I (tr. Bosworth 1999); the 'Kārnāmag ī Ardaxšīr'; Touraj Daryaee, 'Sasanian Persia' (2009).

entries.label: Shapur I and the captured emperors
entries.hint: Shapur I beat three Roman emperors — Gordian III died on campaign in 244, Philip bought peace, and Valerian was taken alive near Edessa in 260 and kept as a living trophy. Shapur cut the great trilingual record of it into the rock at Naqsh-e Rostam, and resettled the tens of thousands he deported from Antioch and Syria in new cities near Ctesiphon and at Gondeshapur.
entries.note: the 'Res Gestae Divi Saporis' (the Ka'ba-ye Zartosht inscription); the Naqsh-e Rostam reliefs; Michael Dodgeon & Samuel Lieu, 'The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars' (1991).

entries.label: Shapur II — the long war and the first persecution
entries.hint: Shapur II reigned seventy years. He won back the districts Rome had taken in 298, failed three times to storm Nisibis, and in 363 trapped the Emperor Julian's invasion below Ctesiphon; Julian died in the retreat and the treaty handed Persia Nisibis, Singara and five provinces. From 340 he ran the empire's first great persecution of Christians, now suspected as agents of a Christian Rome.
entries.note: Ammianus Marcellinus XVIII–XXV; Sozomen, 'Ecclesiastical History' II.9–14 on the persecution; the 'Acts of the Persian Martyrs'.

entries.label: The fifth-century kings and the Hephthalite disaster
entries.hint: A century of mixed fortune: Yazdegerd I made peace with Rome and eased the pressure on the Christians, letting them organise a church; his son Bahram V, raised among the Arabs of al-Hira, is the huntsman-king of Persian legend. Then the eastern nomads, the Hephthalites, broke the empire's army and killed King Peroz in 484, forcing years of tribute and destabilising the throne.
entries.note: al-Tabari I; the Synod of 410 acts (Yazdegerd I); Procopius, 'Wars' I.3–4 on Peroz and the Hephthalites.

entries.label: Kavad I and the Mazdakite crisis
entries.hint: Kavad backed — or used — the preacher Mazdak, whose movement demanded the sharing out of wealth and undercut the nobles and the clergy. The establishment deposed and jailed him in 496; he escaped to the Hephthalites and came back with an army to reclaim the throne. His son Khosrow ended the affair by massacring the Mazdakites, and inherited a nobility that had been badly frightened.
entries.note: al-Tabari I; Patricia Crone, 'Kavad's Heresy and Mazdak's Revolt' (Iran 1991).

entries.label: Khosrow I Anushirvan — the great reforms
entries.hint: Khosrow I rebuilt the state on the ruins Mazdak left. He had the Sawad surveyed field by field and replaced the crop-share with a fixed cash tax; he broke the great nobles' military monopoly by paying and equipping a royal cavalry and splitting the command four ways; and he built a court culture — the translations, Gondeshapur, the Book of Kings. He also sacked Antioch in 540 and deported it wholesale.
entries.note: al-Tabari I; Procopius, 'Wars' II; Zeev Rubin, 'The Reforms of Khusro Anushirwan' (1995).

entries.label: Khosrow II Parviz and the last great war
entries.hint: Khosrow II overran the whole Roman East — Syria, Jerusalem and the True Cross in 614, Egypt by 619, an army at the walls of Constantinople in 626. Then Heraclius marched the other way, through Armenia and down into the Sawad, won at Nineveh in 627, and burned the royal palace at Dastagird. Khosrow was overthrown and killed by his own son in 628, and the dynasty fell into four years of coups.
entries.note: the 'Chronicon Paschale'; Theophylact Simocatta; Walter Kaegi, 'Heraclius, Emperor of Byzantium' (2003).

entries.label: Asōristān — the heart of Ērānšahr
entries.hint: Lowland Mesopotamia was the province the Persians called Asōristān and, in a phrase the sources use, 'the heart of Ērānšahr'. It held the capital, the greatest concentration of people and irrigated land in the empire, and by the seventh century it yielded well over half the crown's cash revenue. It was ruled directly through the court, not farmed out to a vassal — the one indispensable province.
entries.note: the 'Šahrestānīhā ī Ērānšahr'; Michael Morony, 'Iraq after the Muslim Conquest' (1984); the tax figures in al-Tabari and Ibn Khurradadhbih.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Shapur's three triumphs over Rome and the fall of Hatra, the Roman counterstroke and the peace of 298, Julian's death before Ctesiphon, the sack of Antioch, Heraclius in the Sawad, and al-Qadisiyya and the fall of the capital

entries.label: Shapur's three triumphs and the fall of Hatra
entries.hint: Ardashir took Hatra around 240 and razed the shrine-city that had twice held off Rome. His son Shapur then won the greatest run of victories any Persian king ever had over Rome: a dead emperor in 244, a bought peace, the storm of Antioch, and in 260 the capture of the Emperor Valerian himself with his army near Edessa. The Palmyrene Odaenathus, not Rome, drove Shapur back to Ctesiphon.
entries.note: the 'Res Gestae Divi Saporis'; the Bishapur and Naqsh-e Rostam reliefs; Dodgeon & Lieu (1991).

entries.label: The Roman counterstroke and the peace of 298
entries.hint: The Emperor Carus sacked Ctesiphon in 283, and in 298 Galerius routed King Narseh, captured his harem and treasury, and dictated terms: Rome took five provinces east of the Tigris and made Nisibis the sole legal crossing-point for trade. It was the high-water mark of Roman Mesopotamia, and it held for sixty years until Shapur II tore it up.
entries.note: the 'Panegyrici Latini'; Peter Brennan on the Treaty of Nisibis; Ammianus XXV.

entries.label: Julian dies before Ctesiphon
entries.hint: The Emperor Julian brought an army of sixty thousand down the Euphrates to end the Persian problem for good. He beat the defenders under the walls of Ctesiphon but could not take the city, burned his own boats, and turned back up the Tigris harried the whole way. A skirmish wound killed him on 26 June; his successor Jovian bought the army's escape by ceding Nisibis and the five provinces.
entries.note: Ammianus Marcellinus XXIII–XXV; Libanius, 'Oration' 18.

entries.label: The sack of Antioch and the deportation
entries.hint: Breaking the 'Eternal Peace' of 532, Khosrow I marched into Syria in 540, stormed Antioch, and carried its whole population back east to a new city he built for them beside Ctesiphon — 'Khosrow's Better-than-Antioch' — with its own hippodrome and its own bath. The great cities of the Roman East learned that the peace on the frontier was only ever a pause.
entries.note: Procopius, 'Wars' II.8–14; the deportee city in al-Tabari I and the Arabic 'al-Rumiyya'.

entries.label: Heraclius in the Sawad
entries.hint: After twenty years in which Khosrow II conquered the entire Roman East, the Emperor Heraclius gambled everything on a strike at the Persian core. He came through Armenia, wintered in Albania, and in December 627 destroyed the last Persian field army on the old battlefield of Nineveh, then burned Khosrow's palace at Dastagird. The king was murdered weeks later. Both empires were now bankrupt and exhausted.
entries.note: Theophanes, 'Chronographia' AM 6117–6118; the 'Chronicon Paschale'; Kaegi (2003).

entries.label: al-Qadisiyya and the fall of Ctesiphon
entries.hint: Arab columns raided lower Iraq from 633; al-Hira submitted at once. In November 636, on the desert edge near al-Qadisiyya, a three-day battle destroyed the main Persian army and killed its commander Rustam. Ctesiphon — al-Madā'in — fell the following spring, its treasury and the great vault taken; the rout at Nihavand in 642 ended organised resistance. The last king fled east and was murdered in 651.
entries.note: al-Tabari I (tr. Friedmann 1992, 'The Battle of al-Qādisiyyah'); al-Baladhuri, 'Futūh al-Buldān'.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The Sawad as the heart of Ērānšahr and its richest tax base, Ctesiphon the greatest city of the West, Khosrow I's cadastral tax reform, the Zoroastrian state and the four estates, the protected communities under their own heads, and the marzbans and dihqans

entries.label: The Sawad and the crown revenue
entries.hint: Lowland Iraq — the Sawad, 'the black land' of dense cultivation — was the empire's fiscal engine. It carried the largest population and the greatest stretch of irrigated ground in Ērānšahr and, by the last century of Sasanian rule, produced more cash for the treasury than all the Iranian provinces together. Losing it, as the last kings found, meant losing the war.
entries.note: Michael Morony, 'Iraq after the Muslim Conquest' (1984); Robert McC. Adams, 'Land Behind Baghdad' (1965).

entries.label: Ctesiphon — al-Madā'in, 'the Cities'
entries.hint: The capital was not one city but a cluster on both banks of the Tigris — Ctesiphon, the rebuilt Veh-Ardashir, the deportee towns — that the Arabs would call al-Madā'in, 'the Cities'. Contemporaries reckoned it the greatest city between the Mediterranean and China: the White Palace, the arsenals, the mint, the treasury, the great audience hall under its brick vault.
entries.note: the excavations of the German Ctesiphon expedition (Reuther 1930); al-Tabari and al-Khatib al-Baghdadi on al-Madā'in.

entries.label: Khosrow I's cadastral tax
entries.hint: Khosrow I had the land of the Sawad surveyed — the area measured, the date-palms and olive and vine stocks counted — and replaced the old share of the standing crop with a fixed tax in silver, due in three instalments, plus a graded poll tax that exempted the nobility, the soldiers and the clergy. The Arab conquerors kept the system almost unchanged, and it became the fiscal backbone of the Caliphate.
entries.note: al-Tabari I; Zeev Rubin, 'The Reforms of Khusro Anushirwan' (1995); Fred Donner, 'The Early Islamic Conquests' (1981).

entries.label: Throne and altar
entries.hint: Sasanian doctrine held that kingship and religion were twin brothers, neither able to stand without the other. The empire had a state church — Zoroastrianism, with a chief priest, the mowbedān mowbed, ranking near the throne — a fixed order of four estates, priests, warriors, scribes and producers, and a readiness, sharpest under the priest Kartir, to persecute Jews, Christians, Manichaeans and Buddhists as enemies of the order.
entries.note: the 'Letter of Tansar'; the Kartir inscriptions (Naqsh-e Rostam, Sar Mashhad); Touraj Daryaee, 'Sasanian Persia' (2009).

entries.label: The protected communities under their own heads
entries.hint: The crown dealt with its Jews and Christians as bodies, not individuals: each had a recognised head — the exilarch for the Jews, the catholicos for the Church of the East — who answered to the King of Kings, kept internal order, ran the community courts, and delivered a collective tax. It was self-government under a ceiling, punctuated by persecution, and Islam would formalise it as the dhimma.
entries.note: Richard Payne, 'A State of Mixture: Christians, Zoroastrians, and Iranian Political Culture in Late Antiquity' (2015); Geoffrey Herman, 'A Prince without a Kingdom: The Exilarch in the Sasanian Era' (2012).

entries.label: The marzbans and the dihqans
entries.hint: The empire's grip on the ground ran through two layers: the marzbans, military governors of the frontier marches, and below them the dihqāns — the class of village landlords who lived in fortified houses, assessed and gathered the tax, and kept the local registers. When the Arabs came, the dihqāns of the Sawad changed masters and kept their jobs; they staffed the early Islamic administration for a century.
entries.note: Ahmad Tafazzoli, 'Sasanian Society' (2000); Michael Morony, 'Iraq after the Muslim Conquest' (1984).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The Church of the East organised under a catholicos at Seleucia-Ctesiphon, the academies of Sura and Pumbedita and the redaction of the Talmud, Zoroastrianism as the state church, Mazdak's revolt, Mani, and the Mandaeans and the pagan survivals

entries.label: A church organised under the King of Kings
entries.hint: With royal permission the bishops of the empire met at Seleucia-Ctesiphon in 410, adopted the Nicene creed and canons, and put a single head — the catholicos of the capital — over the whole church. In 424 they declared themselves answerable to no Western patriarch, and by 486 they had embraced the strict two-natures Christology that outsiders called Nestorian and allowed their clergy to marry. It became the great missionary church of Asia.
entries.note: the 'Synodicon Orientale' (ed. Chabot 1902); Sebastian Brock, 'The Church of the East in the Sasanian Empire' (2000).

entries.label: Sura and Pumbedita and the making of the Talmud
entries.hint: Rav founded a school at Sura around 220 and Shmuel taught at Nehardea, later Pumbedita; for three centuries the sages of these two academies argued the law clause by clause, gathering twice a year for the kallah assemblies. Out of that debate came the Babylonian Talmud, edited around 500 and polished by the next generation — and with it Babylonia's standing as the senior authority of the Jewish world.
entries.note: David Weiss Halivni, 'The Formation of the Babylonian Talmud' (2013); Jeffrey Rubenstein, 'The Culture of the Babylonian Talmud' (2003).

entries.label: Zoroastrianism written down
entries.hint: Under the Sasanians the Zoroastrian priesthood, for the first time, put its scripture into writing — inventing an alphabet precise enough to fix the sound of the Avesta — and built up the Zand, the Middle Persian commentary, alongside it. The great royal fires burned in the provinces, the calendar was theirs, and the mowbeds' influence over the court reached its peak under the last kings.
entries.note: Mary Boyce, 'Zoroastrians: Their Religious Beliefs and Practices' (1979); Prods Oktor Skjærvø on the Avestan alphabet.

entries.label: Mazdak and the sharing of wealth
entries.hint: Mazdak preached that hoarding was the root of strife and that wealth — and, his enemies said, wives — should be shared out. In a decade of famine and a weak monarchy the message spread, granaries were opened, and King Kavad seemed for a time to back it against his own nobles. The reaction was savage: Khosrow I had the Mazdakites rounded up and killed. The idea kept surfacing in Iranian revolts for centuries.
entries.note: al-Tabari I; al-Shahrastani, 'al-Milal wa-l-Nihal'; Patricia Crone, 'Kavad's Heresy and Mazdak's Revolt' (1991).

entries.label: Mani and the religion of light
entries.hint: Mani, born near Ctesiphon in 216, taught a dualist faith of light trapped in matter, drew on Jewish, Christian, Zoroastrian and Buddhist ideas, wrote his own scriptures and illustrated them, and preached before Shapur I. Bahram I had him executed around 277. His church went underground in Iran but spread across the Roman Empire, Egypt, Central Asia and, eventually, deep into China.
entries.note: the 'Cologne Mani Codex'; Samuel Lieu, 'Manichaeism in the Later Roman Empire and Medieval China' (1985).

entries.label: Mandaeans, Miaphysites and pagans
entries.hint: The religious ground stayed crowded. The Mandaeans — the last surviving gnostics, still there today — kept their river baptisms on the southern canals; a rival West Syrian church grew up among the Antioch deportees; the philosophers of Harran kept an old star-cult alive; and under house floors across the Sawad people buried clay bowls inscribed with spells against demons in Jewish, Christian and Mandaic Aramaic.
entries.note: Kevin van Bladel, 'From Sasanian Mandaeans to Ṣābians of the Marshes' (2017); Shaul Shaked & others, 'Aramaic Bowl Spells' (2013– ).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Syriac literature and the schools of Nisibis and Edessa, the Talmud as a literary monument, Sasanian rock relief and silver, the Book of Kings compiled at court, and the great vault of Ctesiphon

entries.label: The schools of Edessa and Nisibis
entries.hint: Edessa's 'School of the Persians' trained clergy for the church across the border until the Roman authorities closed it in 489 for its Nestorian teaching. Its masters crossed into Persia and refounded it at Nisibis under Narsai, with written statutes, a fixed curriculum of scripture and its commentary, and a boarding community of hundreds. For two centuries it was the intellectual centre of the Church of the East.
entries.note: the 'Statutes of the School of Nisibis' (ed. Vööbus 1961); Adam Becker, 'Fear of God and the Beginning of Wisdom' (2006).

entries.label: The Talmud as a literary monument
entries.hint: The Babylonian Talmud is built as an argument: a line of the older law, then generations of objection, answer, counter-case and resolution, stitched together by an anonymous editorial voice and running from strict jurisprudence into folklore, medicine and legend in the same breath. In sheer size and in reach it is the largest and most consequential work produced anywhere in the late antique Near East.
entries.note: David Weiss Halivni, 'The Formation of the Babylonian Talmud' (tr. 2013); Shamma Friedman on the anonymous stratum.

entries.label: The king in rock and silver
entries.hint: Sasanian kingship advertised itself in a fixed set of images — the god handing the king his ring of rule, the king spearing a Roman or a lion — cut into cliffs, hammered into silver-gilt dishes, and woven into silks patterned with pearl-bordered roundels. The style was studied and copied everywhere it reached, from the mosaics of Byzantium to the wall-paintings of Tang China, and it fed straight into early Islamic art.
entries.note: Prudence Harper, 'The Royal Hunter: Art of the Sasanian Empire' (1978); the silver plate collections of the Hermitage and the Metropolitan Museum.

entries.label: The Book of Kings
entries.hint: The court at Ctesiphon kept and shaped the Xwadāy-nāmag, the 'Book of Lords' — the official chronicle of Iran's kings and heroes from the first man to the reigning Khosrow, part history and part epic. Translated into Arabic within a century of the conquest, it is the channel through which the whole Persian legendary past reached Ferdowsi and became the Shāhnāma. The keeper of Iran's national memory sat in the Sawad.
entries.note: the reconstruction in al-Tabari and al-Tha'alibi; A. Shapur Shahbazi, 'On the Xwadāy-nāmag' (1990).

entries.label: The great vault of Ctesiphon
entries.hint: The audience hall of the palace at Ctesiphon was roofed by a single parabolic vault of baked brick, about thirty-seven metres high and twenty-six across, raised without any wooden framework by leaning each course against the last. It is the largest brick arch of the pre-modern world, and part of it still stands. Arab poets writing three centuries later used its ruin as the image of fallen empire.
entries.note: Oscar Reuther, 'Die Ausgrabungen der deutschen Ktesiphon-Expedition' (1930); al-Buhturi's ode on the Aywān of Kisrā.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Gondeshapur and its medicine, the translation movement under Khosrow I gathering Greek and Indian learning, the dialectic of the rabbinic academies, Syriac Aristotelian scholarship, and the royal astronomical tables

entries.label: Gondeshapur
entries.hint: Shapur I settled his Antiochene captives in a new city in Khuzestan, on the edge of the Sawad, and over the following centuries it became the empire's medical centre — Greek, Syriac and Indian traditions taught together, with a hospital attached and a dynasty of court physicians, the Bukhtishu, running it. When the Abbasids built their House of Wisdom and their Baghdad hospital, Gondeshapur was the working model they drew on.
entries.note: Lutz Richter-Bernburg, 'Gondēšāpūr' in Encyclopaedia Iranica; the Bukhtishu family in Ibn Abi Usaybia.

entries.label: The learning brought to Khosrow's court
entries.hint: When Justinian closed the Academy of Athens in 529, seven Neoplatonist philosophers took refuge at Khosrow I's court before returning under a treaty clause protecting them. The king also sent his physician Borzuya to India, who came back with the animal-fable book that became Kalila wa-Dimna, the game of chess, and Indian astronomy. Greek logic and medicine were being turned into Middle Persian and Syriac at the same time.
entries.note: Agathias, 'Histories' II.28–31; the preface to 'Kalīla wa-Dimna'; Dimitri Gutas, 'Greek Thought, Arabic Culture' (1998).

entries.label: The dialectic of the academies
entries.hint: The method of the Babylonian academies was argument for its own sake as much as for the result: take a ruling, raise every possible objection, test it against invented cases, force the contradictions to resolve. The Talmud preserves the give-and-take rather than just the verdict. It bred a distinctive cast of mind — analytic, adversarial, comfortable with unresolved tension — that shaped Jewish learning permanently.
entries.note: Jeffrey Rubenstein, 'The Culture of the Babylonian Talmud' (2003); David Kraemer, 'The Mind of the Talmud' (1990).

entries.label: Syriac, the bridge from Greek to Arabic
entries.hint: Syriac scholars in the Sasanian and border lands translated and digested the Greek inheritance a full century before the Arabs arrived: Sergius of Reshaina put Galen and Aristotle's logic into Syriac around 500, Paul the Persian wrote a logic for Khosrow I, and the medical and philosophical compendia multiplied. The great Abbasid translation movement began by hiring these Syriac Christians and their descendants.
entries.note: Henri Hugonnard-Roche, 'La logique d'Aristote du grec au syriaque' (2004); Dimitri Gutas (1998).

entries.label: The royal astronomical tables
entries.hint: Court astronomers at Ctesiphon compiled the Zīg-ī Šahriyārān, the 'Tables of the Kings' — a working handbook for computing the positions of the sun, moon and planets that folded Ptolemaic geometry together with Indian parameters. Revised again under the last king, it was the starting point for the first Islamic astronomical tables and the whole 'Persian' branch of medieval astronomy.
entries.note: E. S. Kennedy, 'A Survey of Islamic Astronomical Tables' (1956); David Pingree on the Persian solar-apogee observation (1965).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The Nahrawan and the Sawad's agriculture at its historic peak, the richest tax base in the world, the silk trade and the Gulf ports, the cities peopled with Roman deportees, and the fire-altar drachm

entries.label: The Nahrawan
entries.hint: The Sasanians dug — and Khosrow I finished — a trunk canal that ran some three hundred kilometres down the east side of the Tigris, fed from the Diyala, watering a swathe of country east of Ctesiphon that had never been farmed before. Archaeological survey shows the Sawad's cultivated area and its population reaching a peak in these centuries that it would not touch again until modern times.
entries.note: Robert McC. Adams, 'Land Behind Baghdad' (1965); Peter Verkinderen, 'Waterways of Iraq and Iran in the Early Islamic Period' (2015).

entries.label: The richest tax base in the world
entries.hint: The Arab historians preserve the last Sasanian assessment of the Sawad — well over two hundred million silver drachms a year, more than any other land the conquerors knew. The fields grew wheat and barley, and also rice, dates, cotton, sesame, flax, wine and sugar cane newly brought from India. Every empire that could reach Iraq wanted it for this, and the ones that held it were rich.
entries.note: al-Tabari I and Ibn Khurradadhbih on the Sawad assessment; Michael Morony, 'Iraq after the Muslim Conquest' (1984).

entries.label: The silk monopoly and the Gulf ports
entries.hint: Persia stood between Byzantium and China and made both pay for it: raw silk came west only through Persian hands and at a Persian price, and two of the wars with Byzantium turned partly on the trade. Persian merchants ran the sea leg themselves — colonies on the Gulf coast, factors in Ceylon, ships to south China — while Byzantium tried and failed to route around them through Ethiopia.
entries.note: Procopius, 'Wars' I.20; Cosmas Indicopleustes, 'Christian Topography' XI; Étienne de la Vaissière, 'Sogdian Traders' (2005).

entries.label: The deportee cities and their crafts
entries.hint: Deporting a captured city was, among other things, industrial policy. The tens of thousands moved from Antioch and Syria by Shapur I and again by Khosrow I were resettled in purpose-built towns near the capital and in Khuzestan, and they brought silk-weaving, glass, mosaic, and Roman hydraulic engineering with them. The skills stayed and spread; the crafts of early Islamic Iraq were partly Roman transplants.
entries.note: al-Tabari I; Erich Kettenhofen, 'Deportations' in Encyclopaedia Iranica.

entries.label: The drachm that became the dirham
entries.hint: The Sasanian silver drachm — thin, broad, the king's bust on one side and a fire altar with two attendants on the other — was struck in immense quantity at dozens of mints and circulated far beyond the empire. The Arab conquerors kept minting it, adding a word of Arabic, for fifty years; when they finally issued a purely Islamic dirham in 697 they kept its weight exactly.
entries.note: Rika Gyselen, 'Arab-Sasanian Coppers' and the Sasanian mint corpus; Stephen Album, 'Checklist of Islamic Coins' (2011).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The pitched-brick vault of the Taq Kasra, the engineering of the three-hundred-kilometre Nahrawan, the norias of Hit and the piedmont qanats, and the pontoon bridges and the posting road

entries.label: The pitched-brick vault
entries.hint: The builders of the great hall at Ctesiphon raised its vault without any timber centering: each ring of bricks was laid leaning back against the one before, set in fast gypsum mortar, so the arch grew slice by slice from the two ends. Thick brick haunches took the outward thrust. It was the old Mesopotamian answer to a treeless land, pushed to its structural limit.
entries.note: Oscar Reuther (1930); K. A. C. Creswell, 'Early Muslim Architecture' vol. I (1969), on the technique's afterlife.

entries.label: The engineering of the Nahrawan
entries.hint: The Nahrawan needed a masonry intake to draw and control the Diyala's flow, dozens of gated offtakes feeding the field canals, a tail escape back to the Tigris to shed floodwater, and a standing corvée to dredge it. It worked for four centuries. When the political order that organised the labour broke down in the tenth and eleventh centuries the canal silted, and the land it watered went back to desert.
entries.note: Robert McC. Adams, 'Land Behind Baghdad' (1965); Peter Verkinderen (2015).

entries.label: The norias of Hit and the lifting of water
entries.hint: Where the river ran below its fields the Sawad lifted water mechanically: the giant undershot wheels at Hit on the Euphrates, turning in the current and tipping water into elevated channels; the ox-driven chain-of-pots elsewhere; and, along the piedmont, qanats — gently sloping tunnels that carried groundwater to the surface by gravity. The kit was ancient; the scale under the Sasanians was new.
entries.note: Thorkild Schiøler, 'Roman and Islamic Water-Lifting Wheels' (1973); the norias of Hit in the Arab geographers.

entries.label: The bridges and the royal road
entries.hint: Ctesiphon crossed the Tigris on bridges of boats that could be broken up when an enemy approached. From the capital the royal highway ran east over the passes to the Iranian plateau and west toward Syria, with posting stations and relays of horses for the king's messengers — the network the Arabs took over and called the barīd.
entries.note: Ammianus Marcellinus XXIV.6 (the bridge); Ibn Khurradadhbih, 'Kitāb al-Masālik wa-l-Mamālik', on the roads and the barid.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The three-century war with Byzantium over the same ground, the Church of the East reaching India and China, al-Hira and the Lakhmid buffer, the Jewish world centred on Babylonia, and the Sasanian apparatus passing whole to Islam

entries.label: The war over the same ground
entries.hint: For three and a half centuries Rome and Persia fought over a narrow band of upper Mesopotamia — Nisibis, Dara, Amida, the Khabur line — in a rhythm of siege, treaty, subsidy and renewed war. Diplomats called the two courts the eyes of the world; each paid the other when it suited. The frontier moved a little each war and settled roughly where the modern Syria–Turkey–Iraq borders now run.
entries.note: Geoffrey Greatrex & Samuel Lieu, 'The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars, Part II' (2002).

entries.label: The Church of the East reaches India and China
entries.hint: From its base in the Sawad, the Church of the East spread along the trade routes: bishoprics across Iran to Merv and Herat, a metropolitan for the Christians of the Malabar coast of India, missions into the Turkic steppe, and — the year before the Arabs took Ctesiphon — a mission arriving in the Tang capital, later commemorated on the Xi'an stele. Syriac was its language from Iraq to China.
entries.note: the 'Xi'an stele' (781); Ian Gillman & Hans-Joachim Klimkeit, 'Christians in Asia before 1500' (1999).

entries.label: al-Hira and the Lakhmid shield
entries.hint: On the desert edge below Ctesiphon the Arab kings of al-Hira held a Christian, poetry-loving court and served Persia as a buffer and a listening-post facing Arabia and Byzantine Syria. Khosrow II abolished the kingdom around 602 and put a governor in its place — and a few years later an Arab tribal force beat a Persian army at Dhu Qar. The frontier the Lakhmids had watched now lay open.
entries.note: al-Tabari I; Isabel Toral-Niehoff, 'Al-Ḥīra: Eine arabische Kulturmetropole im spätantiken Kontext' (2014).

entries.label: The Jewish world tilts to Babylonia
entries.hint: Over these centuries the centre of gravity of Judaism moved decisively from a broken Roman Palestine to the large, prosperous, self-governing community of the Sawad. Students crossed to study at Sura and Pumbedita, the exilarch's authority ran across the diaspora, and the rulings of the Babylonian sages began going out as written answers to questions from communities as far west as North Africa and Spain.
entries.note: Isaiah Gafni, 'Land, Center and Diaspora' (1997); Robert Brody, 'The Geonim of Babylonia' (1998).

entries.label: The apparatus passes to Islam
entries.hint: The Arab conquerors planted their garrison cities, Kufa and Basra, beside the old capital region and later built Baghdad thirty kilometres up the Tigris. They kept the Sasanian tax survey and the kharāg, employed the dihqāns to run it, adopted the drachm, the government departments, the postal road and much of the court ceremonial. Islamic Iraq was built on Sasanian foundations with the walls still standing.
entries.note: Michael Morony, 'Iraq after the Muslim Conquest' (1984); Hugh Kennedy, 'The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates' (2004).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: Mesopotamia the heart of a great power again for the first time since Hammurabi, the plural society of three institutionalised communities, the two exhausted empires when the Arabs came, and early Islamic Iraq as Sasanian Iraq renamed

entries.label: The heart of a great power
entries.hint: For the first time since the Old Babylonian kings a thousand years before — and the last time before the Abbasids six centuries later — Mesopotamia was the centre from which a world empire was ruled, not its edge or its province. The King of Kings sat at Ctesiphon; the Sawad paid for the wars; the roads ran outward from here. Iraq spent four centuries as a heartland rather than a frontier.
entries.note: Josef Wiesehöfer, 'Ancient Persia' (2001); Michael Morony, 'Iraq after the Muslim Conquest' (1984).

entries.label: Many faiths, each with a head
entries.hint: A Zoroastrian state ruled a population that was mostly not Zoroastrian — Christian, Jewish, Manichaean, Mandaean, pagan. Each large community had a recognised leader who answered to the crown, kept internal order and delivered a collective tax. It was hierarchy, not tolerance, and it could turn to persecution; but it was also the working model of the plural, self-administering communities that Islam would inherit as the dhimma.
entries.note: Richard Payne, 'A State of Mixture' (2015); Michael Morony (1984).

entries.label: Two exhausted empires
entries.hint: The war of 603–628 had been total: Persia had conquered and lost the whole Roman East, Byzantine armies had burned the Sasanian palaces, and both treasuries were empty and both dynasties discredited. When the Arab armies came out of the desert a few years later, neither power could field a defence that would hold. The speed of the conquest is half explained by the state of what it conquered.
entries.note: James Howard-Johnston, 'Witnesses to a World Crisis' (2010); Walter Kaegi, 'Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests' (1992).

entries.label: Sasanian Iraq becomes Islamic Iraq
entries.hint: The conquest replaced the ruler, the state religion and — over centuries — the language. It kept almost everything else: the capital region, the tax survey and the cash kharāg, the dihqān administrators, the coin standard, the postal roads, the canal network, the court ceremonial. The continuity from the last Sasanian century into the first Islamic one is closer than the change of masters suggests.
entries.note: Michael Morony, 'Iraq after the Muslim Conquest' (1984); Chase Robinson, 'Empire and Elites after the Muslim Conquest' (2000).

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The catholicos of the East at the royal city, the head of the academy at Sura or Pumbedita, the dihqan of the village, the deported Antiochene craftsman, and the court physician of Gondeshapur

entries.label: The catholicos of the East
entries.hint: Chosen by the bishops and confirmed — sometimes picked — by the King of Kings, the catholicos lived at the capital and answered for every Christian in the empire: their spokesman at court, the crown's tax-gatherer among them, the judge of last resort in their disputes. In the persecutions the office was lethal; Simeon bar Sabbae and many successors were executed. It was also the head of a church that reached to China.
entries.note: the 'Synodicon Orientale'; the 'History of Mar Aba'; Sebastian Brock (2000).

entries.label: The head of the academy
entries.hint: He presided over one of the two great schools and over the kallah months, when scholars came in from their villages by the thousand to study a tractate together. He ruled on the questions the local courts could not settle, taught the sessions that his students turned into the text of the Talmud, and wrote answers to letters from communities a month's journey away. His title, gaon, would later mean simply 'the authority'.
entries.note: Robert Brody, 'The Geonim of Babylonia and the Shaping of Medieval Jewish Culture' (1998); David Goodblatt, 'Rabbinic Instruction in Sasanian Babylonia' (1975).

entries.label: The dihqan
entries.hint: A landowner of the middling sort — a few hundred hectares, a fortified mudbrick house, a Zoroastrian household — he was the state's man in the village: he assessed the harvest, gathered the district's tax for the marzban, kept the land register, and remembered the boundaries and the genealogies. When the Arabs took over, the job stayed exactly the same and so, for a century, did the families doing it.
entries.note: Ahmad Tafazzoli, 'Sasanian Society' (2000); the dihqāns in Morony (1984).

entries.label: The deported Antiochene
entries.hint: A weaver, or a man who set mosaic floors, marched from Antioch to Mesopotamia after the sack of 540 and resettled in the copy-city Khosrow built for his captives beside Ctesiphon — same street plan, a hippodrome, a bath. He worked his craft for a Persian court, kept his Greek and his Chalcedonian faith among Nestorian neighbours, and passed the skill to sons who were born subjects of the King of Kings.
entries.note: Procopius, 'Wars' II.14; al-Tabari I on the deportee city; Erich Kettenhofen on the deportations.

entries.label: The court physician of Gondeshapur
entries.hint: A Christian trained in the medicine of three worlds — Galen in Syriac, the Indian texts, the local practice — he attended the King of Kings and taught at the hospital city. His family, the Bukhtishu, would go on serving in an unbroken line for two and a half centuries, as physicians first to the last Sasanians and then to the caliphs of Baghdad. The knowledge crossed the conquest without a break.
entries.note: Ibn Abi Usaybia, 'ʿUyūn al-Anbāʾ'; Lutz Richter-Bernburg, 'Boḵtīšuʿ' in Encyclopaedia Iranica.
